failure_mode: Launch abort / all lift motors stopped during VTOL climb on takeoff; team attributes it to the same VTOL AP memory corruption found on v696
contributing: Software release 6.3.0 under regression test
Debug log shows launch aborting with no fault shown in VTOL window

evidence.quote: Flight #4 during take-off all the motors just stopped at around 50-100ft and it just dropped down on its nose
debuglog says says launch is aborting. Another indication that something went wrong on launch.
Same issue as v696. Closed
There is memory corruption in the Config Manager that occurs after 161 TCB task events occur (creation/deletion).

would_settle_it.what: VTOL AP and XCOMM logs at the launch abort: TCB task event count and Config Manager corruption signature matching v696
Team investigation slides and fishbone for 481 (SharePoint)

The Root Cause field only points to VXEP-514, and the Issue Status says it is the same issue as v696, where the team found VTOL AP Config Manager memory corruption after 161 task events. event: During automatic VTOL landing, VXE 558 (USASOC) overshot the PLZ, drifted while descending after the VTOL GPS solution failed its uncertainty checks, and crashed with damage.
failure_mode: GPS uncertainty checks failed on approach, VTOL stopped using GPS, went wings level and descended without position hold, drifting past the PLZ
contributing: GNSS receiver rate issue (GNSS-Rate label, patch planned)
VTOL GPS loss not annunciated to the operator (no VT_FAULT_FAIL_VT or sensor error shown)
Climb Abort, Lift System Fault message after transition
Operator Pause and manual correction attempt near ground

evidence.quote: In that case the vehicle goes to pitch/roll level and descends, so unfortunately this is expected system behavior in the event of GPS loss during approach.
In this particular case, the GPS wasn’t completely failed, it just had some of the uncertainty checks fail.
In that case VTOL won’t use the GPS, and this should have been annunciated to the operators.
AV continued to fly past the PLZ by ~80m while in VTOL.

team_root_cause: GPS loss during approach results in wings level command and vehicle descent.

would_settle_it.what: VTOL GPS fix, satellite count and uncertainty flags against the fixed wing GPS on approach, and why the checks failed (GNSS rate or signal)
Eric Brewer summary plots of the GPS dropout

attachments_read: 21182_RMA Repair Quote for AC VXE-558 - New VXE-694 GOODWILL 6-25-2024.pdf.md
reasoning: The engineers found the VTOL GPS solution failed its uncertainty checks on approach, so the VTOL autopilot stopped using GPS and went level and descended, which is designed behavior. That puts the start of the event in the GPS input, scored as narrowed under the designed-abort rule. Why the GPS checks failed is not shown; the GNSS-Rate label and planned patch suggest the receiver rate issue but this is not stated as proven for this flight.
notes: The Lift System Fault message after transition is not explained in the ticket. RMA-275 only covers the goodwill replacement with VXE-694, no teardown findings. The GNSS-Rate link is from a label and a later comment, not from data on this ticket.

event: During landing, VXE 523 (USASOC) lost GPS, entered dead reckoning, landed in place about 300 m from the PLZ and struck a T-wall with the lift props.
failure_mode: Loss of GPS signal during final descent; vehicle landed at its current position as designed when position control was no longer possible
contributing: Operator suspected a jammer, not confirmed
Landing in place behavior on GPS loss not documented in manual or training (SMUP-49)
Winds 11 kt at ground
Prop strike on T-wall

evidence.quote: FW FDR suggests loss of GPS signal
Note tha DR (Dead Reckoning) is a directive caused by loss of GPS
Right now it won’t dead reckon when GPS is lost while it is in the landing sequence, it will simply land where it is at.
My assumption is that some sort of jammer was turned on and caused the AV to enter DR during its final decent for recovery.

team_root_cause: No Issue. The vehicle landed at the current location because GPS was lost and position control was no longer possible.

would_settle_it.what: GPS satellite count, C/N0 and fix status before the dropout, to tell jamming from receiver or antenna fault

reasoning: The FW flight data and XComm show loss of GPS signal with a dead reckoning directive, and the team states the vehicle lands in place when GPS is lost in the landing sequence. This is a designed response to a degraded GPS input, so it is scored narrowed to GPS. Why GPS was lost (jamming as the operator suspected, or something on board) is not shown.
notes: CSV attachment holds only the flight log column headers (61 rows, data not exported). Plots of the GPS loss are images not in the export.

event: On landing, VXE 592 (MOLSON) overshot the PLZ, aborted the VTOL landing on a low power fault while the lift system stayed engaged, then on a second attempt nose-dived into a moving truck (aircraft loss).
component: VTOL AP GNSS update handling (5 Hz rate) and land abort logic
failure_mode: GNSS update rate caused VTOL attitude errors so transition did not arrest speed; lift power stayed low, XComm triggered a low power fault, and the land abort bug left both autopilots controlling the vehicle
contributing: GNSS receiver rate change causing PLZ overshoot
Land abort bug in LAND_WAITTRANS path (both APs in control)
Customer saw one lift motor slow to start on first transition
Second approach flown by operator after emergency glide indication

evidence.quote: The debug/xcomm event logs indicate the abort was caused by a low power fault. Meaning the lift system did not consume enough power during landing.
The power chart on XComm shows low power (<500W) for a large chunk of the landing which is not normal.
Note that the VTOL low power is caused in large part by the 5hz GPS update rate issue we’ve observed previously.
Due to attitude errors in the VTOL controller, the vehicle does not pitch up far enough on transition and the speed is not arrested.
This land abort occurred during the LAND_WAITTRANS TestLandAbort (LA-02-008-02) code path which has been confirmed to activate the land abort bug.
Transitioned from glide to VTOL. 3 of 4 motors turned on. The 4th looked like it was trying to initiate.

team_root_cause:
- PLZ Overshoot caused by the GNSS receiver rate change.
- Land Abort bug resulted in both APs trying to control the vehicle.

Both are known issues and are being addressed in the upcoming SW release.

would_settle_it.what: XComm power and event log chart (SharePoint) confirming low lift power and the abort timing
VTOL log at the incident: attitude error, GNSS rate, and whether one lift motor failed to start

reasoning: XComm logs show lift power under 500 W for much of the landing, which tripped the low power fault and the land abort. Brewer ties the low power to the 5 Hz GNSS update rate causing VTOL attitude errors so the vehicle did not pitch up and kept too much wing lift, and Scherer shows the abort ran through the code path known to leave both autopilots in control. Both mechanisms are named by log evidence, so this is determined, medium because the logs themselves are not in the export.
notes: The customer report of one lift motor slow to start on the first transition is not addressed by the team. VXEP-1291 is a later (2025) crash of the same tail and was not read as it is a separate event. RMA-292 (gimbal repair) not read; not about cause.

event: On VXE 674 (and VXE 490) on the ground, E140ZG2 gimbals disturbed the fixed wing magnetometer by up to 30 to 40 degrees as the gimbal panned, causing launch wizard mag check problems; no flight incident.
component: E140ZG2 gimbal (lens cap magnet or gimbal motor magnetic field)
failure_mode: Magnetic field from the gimbal near the fuselage avionics disturbs the fixed wing AP magnetometer heading as the gimbal pans
contributing: Fixed wing magnetometer located near the payload
Possible ground loop through conductive gimbal mount (VXEP-813)
Two random Epsilon software crashes seen during testing

evidence.quote: We tried another gimbal (sn6086). Similar results. Removed gimbal completely and appears mags are happy.
The interference exists with the cable unplugged, so it is the magnetic fields of the motor interfering with the mag.
There is a magnet in the lens for the cap to put in place.
Per discussion we are closing this incident, as it is either the magnets in the E140 face (for cover mounting), or a possible ground loop
Zero MAG issues or anomalies were experienced during these flights.

team_view_in_comments: as it is either the magnets in the E140 face (for cover mounting), or a possible ground loop (which is another incident), linked.

would_settle_it.file: E140 with lens cap magnets removed
would_settle_it.what: Repeat the pan test with the face magnets removed and the cable unplugged to split magnet field from motor field
Field map around the gimbal with and without it installed, as proposed in the 8/6 email
Further ground loop test results with non-conductive mounts (in progress)

reasoning: Swap tests showed the effect with two different E140 gimbals on two aircraft and it went away with the gimbal removed; an E95 did not cause it, and Riga reproduced it. Chapman reports the interference remained with the cable unplugged, which points to a permanent magnetic field (lens cap magnet or motor magnets) rather than a powered ground loop, but VXEP-813 later saw no mag issues with non-conductive mounts, so a ground loop remains a credible alternative. This narrows to the E140 gimbal without settling which part.
notes: Canceled ticket, folded into VXEP-813. The cable unplugged result is reported from memory. Gimbal 6084 was on a 3D printed (non-conductive) mount yet still interfered, which argues against the ground loop for this case. No flight damage occurred.

event: VXE 556 (USASOC, 3rd SFG) was commanded GoTo IP4 at about 2,950 ft AGL, began VTOL landing at about 2,550 ft, ran the HLB out of energy and crashed from about 1,200 ft.
component: GoTo IP4 command skipping the IP2 descending orbit
failure_mode: Operator GoTo IP4 from cruise altitude caused VTOL transition far above the 300 ft standard; HLB depleted during the long vertical descent; abort is not available once in VTOL landing
contributing: GCS had no warning or lockout for VTOL landing from an unsupported altitude (GCSS-362)
Firmware had no energy check before transition (FS2-2318, canceled)
Operators believed they had commanded RTB

evidence.quote: This caused the vehicle to skip IP2. IP2 is a descending orbit that is critical to ensure that the transition to VTOL Landing occurs at a safe altitude.
The VTOL battery system ran out of energy as expected after a VTOL Landing from this altitude.
Here is an image that shows the AGL altitude at the time of the VTOL transition (~3,937 s). The vehicle is ~2,552 ft AGL.
Change active waypoint: : Mission: Primary LZ  Waypoint: 4

team_root_cause:
Closed: Operator error
@David Grosher this doesn’t seem like a total root cause. Yes, the operator should not have executed a VTOL landing at 2500ft, but robust software should also warn/not allow a VTOL landing to start that high.  Seems like that is acknowledged in the CA. More info on what the operator error was would also be useful in that field.
reasoning: The XComm and GCS event logs show a GoTo IP4 command and no RTB command, and the altitude plot puts the VTOL transition at about 2,552 ft AGL. The team found the HLB did not fail but ran out of energy as expected from that height. The failure started with the operator command, with the lack of a GCS altitude or energy check as a contributor.
notes: Customer statement says 1200 ft transition, verbal report 2500 ft; logs show about 2,552 ft at transition and 1,200 ft is likely where lift was lost. FS2-2102 moved to GCSS-362. Root Cause field also holds an editorial note that software should warn.

event: During a 6.3.2 software regression flight test, VXE 696 cut its VTOL lift motors at about 80 ft on takeoff and crashed.
component: VTOL AP Config Manager (TCB task table memory corruption)
failure_mode: Memory corruption in the Config Manager after 161 TCB task create/delete events, cutting VTOL during takeoff
contributing: Dynamic memory allocation from task creation and deletion over a flight
Same failure seen earlier on v481 (VXEP-429)

evidence.quote: [12:28 PM] Ruysser Gabler - VTOL cut on take off again. at 80 ft this time
There is memory corruption in the Config Manager that occurs after 161 TCB task events occur (creation/deletion).
Short term: VTOL AP will be reset by launch wizard. Minor change in TCB trace table to push memory corruption out of critical data space.
Doing a resistance check on the AS150 contact passes, showed 169uohms (limit is 235 uohms). No evidence of solder reflow.

team_root_cause: Issue was identified. There is memory corruption in the Config Manager that occurs after 161 TCB task events occur (creation/deletion).  This could be related to new features but it is unlikely, it is most likely due to the dynamic memory allocation associated with task creation and deletion across the course of a flight.

would_settle_it.what: VTOL AP log showing the Config Manager corruption and the motor cut at takeoff

reasoning: The team identified a specific software mechanism: Config Manager memory corruption after 161 task events, with a matching corrective action on the TCB table. Hardware checks on the AS150 contact and the J4 servo wire found nothing wrong. The mechanism is specific, but the log evidence behind it is not in the export, so confidence is medium.
notes: The launch wizard ADP error seen on the bench was put down to avionics position on the iron bird. VXEP-845 is a teardown/disposal list with no findings.

event: VXE 444 (MARSOC training) kept gaining altitude despite trying to descend, the operator commanded GoTo waypoint 3, and the aircraft began VTOL landing at about 500 ft AGL; no crash reported.
component: Thermals and gusty winds at high density altitude
failure_mode: Aircraft could not bleed off altitude in fixed wing descent (up to about 800 ft altitude error); operator then shortcut the descent so VTOL began high
contributing: Operator GoTo waypoint 3 exited the descending orbit early
Landing pattern checks only 2D position, not altitude, before starting landing

evidence.quote: All sensors appear good, the AV was trying to do everything it could to bleed off altitude (airspeed increase, no throttle, spoiler) but it continued to gain altitude
my only theory is that it is thermals and a windy/gusty environment contributing to the performance issues
It appears that the operator commanded a GoTo waypoint 3 and exited the descent.
The final landing pattern only checks 2d position to confirm that it is close enough for landing and so continued with the landing regardless of the altitude mismatch.
Altitude appears to be normal/ everything agrees on altitude (AV knows where it is)

team_root_cause: Windy/Gusty Environment with thermals that made it difficult for the aircraft to maintain altitude

would_settle_it.what: Wind estimates and vertical air mass motion against commanded descent to confirm thermals

reasoning: Sensors agreed on altitude and the aircraft used every means to descend but kept climbing, and the investigator could only offer thermals and gusty winds as a theory. The high VTOL start was directly caused by the operator GoTo command that skipped the descending orbit, which the investigator called operator impatience. The climb problem is narrowed to the environment with low confidence; the VTOL altitude part is an operator action.
notes: Two parts on one ticket: the altitude holding problem (environment theory, not proven) and the high VTOL start (operator GoTo, shown in XComm log). Plots are images not in the export.

event: During a launch abort test, MCM-only VXE 300 flipped upside down on VTOL takeoff because the VTOL AP pitch estimate was wrong, damaging nosecone, props, tail boom and wingtip.
component: VTOL AP I2C2 driver (unterminated wait loop) hanging GPSParse and sensor tasks
failure_mode: GPSParse task hung on the I2C2 bus and blocked the sensor task, leaving a bad pitch estimate at launch; OGCS launch wizard did not stop the launch
contributing: OGCS/VSM v1.0 launch wizard lacked legacy GCS background checks and launch abort on unusual angles
RTC updates over the I2C2 bus during flight (FS2-2141)
Only GPS time status bit valid at launch

evidence.quote: It looks like the pitch estimate was way off. Which explains the flip on launch.
It also appears that the only valid status bit for GPS was GPS time.
The unterminated while loop in the VTOL code is only used on I2C2 which communicates with the (unused) potentiometer and RTC.
In order to avoid possibility of I2C bus issues communicating with the RTC we’ll set the RTC only post landing
There’s a good reason to believe that the legacy GCS software would have detected a failure of this sort during launch wizard

team_root_cause:
- VTOL AP had the sensor Task blocked and GPSParse task hung on the I2C2 bus. The coupling of the tasks has already been fixed in the 6.3 release. There is still a path for the I2C bus to hang on initialization https://jenaero.atlassian.net/browse/FS2-2142 https://jenaero.atlassian.net/browse/FS2-2143  and a fix for this will be provided in 6.4 along with a change of when the RTC will be allowed to be updated (only after landing) https://jenaero.atlassian.net/browse/FS2-2141 .
- The OGCS failed to prevent launch when issues were detected on the AP itself. A series of critical issues and fixes

would_settle_it.what: VTOL task status at launch showing the I2C2 hang and the GPSParse/sensor task stall

reasoning: The VTOL log shows a badly wrong pitch estimate before launch and only GPS time valid, consistent with the sensor and GPS tasks being stalled. The team traced this to GPSParse hanging on the I2C2 bus, and FS2-2142 identifies the unterminated wait loop on I2C2 (the RTC bus) as the hang path. The OGCS launch wizard then let the launch proceed.
notes: VXEP-526 is a duplicate of this ticket. MS-364 and MS-365 are damage assessments only (all lift motor/ESCs replaced as a precaution after prop strikes). The VTOL event log cut out before the launch event.
